description_full: Motorola Solutions, Inc. provides public safety, government, defense, and enterprise security solutions in the United States, the United Kingdom, Canada, and internationally. It operates in two segments, Products and Systems Integration, and Software and Services. The Products and Systems Integration segment offers a portfolio of infrastructure, devices, accessories, and the implementation and integration of systems, devices, software, and applications for government, including defense, public safety, and enterprise customers who operate private communications systems and video security solutions, as well as manage a mobile workforce. This segment also provides mission critical networks, and video security and access control technologies, including two-way portable and vehicle-mounted radios, video cameras, and accessories; communications network core and central processing software, base stations, consoles, and repeaters; and video analytics, network video management hardware and software, and access control solutions. The Software and Services segment offers public safety and enterprise command center, unified communications applications, mobile video equipment, and video software solutions; repair, technical support, and maintenance services; and monitoring, software updates, and cybersecurity services to government, public safety, and commercial communications networks. It serves hospitality; manufacturing; military and defence; police; air transportation; fire and rescue; stadium; emergency medical services; mining; oil and gas; transportation and logistics; utilities; education; retail; and healthcare industries. The company was formerly known as Motorola, Inc. and changed its name to Motorola Solutions, Inc. in January 2011. Motorola Solutions, Inc. was founded in 1928 and is headquartered in Chicago, Illinois.

financial_summary: Motorola Solutions, Inc. is a large-cap technology business with a $85.1B market cap on $11.7B of annual revenue.
The top line has compounded at +9% over the past three years and +7% annually across the full decade, a respectable pace for a business of this size.
Returns on capital run at 37% against a 8% cost of capital — a 29-point spread that is the clearest signature of an economic moat, with gross margins sitting at 49%.

The business throws off $2.6B in free cash flow — roughly 22 cents on every revenue dollar, which is the owner-earnings figure that actually belongs to shareholders, and cash conversion sits at 1.32× so those profits are backed by real cash.
On the balance sheet, debt is moderate at 2.3× net debt/EBITDA, serviceable in normal conditions but worth watching through a downturn, and interest coverage runs at 9.9×.

Shareholder yield of 2.2% reflects a genuine commitment to returning capital rather than empire-building, and insider ownership is negligible, so management has little personal stake in the long-term outcome.

sect: Its 26% operating margin runs 19pp above the Technology median (7%), a real cost or pricing edge over peers.
Its share of sector profits slightly exceeds its share of revenue (1.09x).
It accounts for 0.3% of sector revenue and 0.3% of sector operating profit.
The sector is fragmented and competitive (HHI 0.03 across 530 companies in the universe; the top four hold 29% of revenue), so pricing power is hard to come by.
mkt: The shares have drifted higher, up 19% over the past year excluding the latest month.
The price sits near the top of its 52-week range, 6% below the high.
With annualised volatility of 25% and a beta of 0.76, it is more defensive than the market, though its beta has shifted (1y -0.10 vs 5y 0.73), so read it loosely.
Liquidity is deep, with about $388.0M traded a day.
In past sell-offs it fell 33% in the 2020 crash, 26% in the 2022 bear market and 80% in 2008.
val: The price sits above its DCF fair value of $307 (margin of safety -68%), so there is no valuation cushion.
The fair-value models disagree (dispersion 25%), and the Monte Carlo range runs $233 to $426 (P10-P90), so treat the estimate as noisy.
On multiples it looks expensive against Technology peers: P/E 41.4 vs 26.7, EV/EBITDA 26.0 vs 16.4 and P/FCF 33.1 vs 25.4 (sector median).
Against its own history it is dear: the EBIT multiple sits 43% above its 10-year median.
Earnings yields are thin: an FCF yield of 3.0% (below the risk-free rate) and an EBIT/EV of 3.1% (vs the 8% bar).
The 11 covering analysts target $527 on average, 2% above the price, well away from the model's fair value.
prof: ROIC of 37% clears the cost of capital of 8.1% by 29pp, the mark of a value creator; returns have swung a lot from year to year (CV 0.72).
It runs a 49% gross margin and converts 22% of revenue into free cash flow.
Earnings quality looks solid: cash conversion of 1.32x.
ROE of 89% is amplified by 8.0x balance-sheet leverage (DuPont), so ROIC is the cleaner read on the business.
Operating margin is running 5pp above its own historical average, a peak-margin risk if conditions normalise.
It spends 8.3% of revenue on R&D and 2.5% on stock compensation (above the 2% gate).
hlth: Leverage is moderate at 2.3x net debt to EBITDA ($1.2B of cash against $9.2B of debt), above the 1.5x gate, with interest covered 9.9x.
No distress or manipulation flags (Altman Z 4.3, in the safe zone).
Goodwill makes up 35% of assets, a soft asset exposed to impairment.
growth: Revenue has compounded at 8.6% over 3 years, 9.5% over 5 years and 7.4% over 10 years, and it has been lumpy (year-to-year swings of 18%).
Net reinvestment is nil (capex and working capital no more than cover depreciation), so fundamental growth is near zero.
Free cash flow has compounded 13.0% a year over five years.
Forward indicators: a book-to-bill of 1.02, a backlog worth 82% of annual revenue and deferred revenue up 17%.
Capex runs only 0.6x depreciation (2.3% of sales), so the asset base is being harvested rather than grown.
own: Insiders hold little stock (0.4%), and institutions hold 92%.
Insiders have only sold over the past year (12 sales, net $8.5M sold).
It returns 2.2% a year to shareholders (1.3% in buybacks and 0.9% in dividends).
It has paid a dividend for 15 consecutive years, raising it 10.8% a year over the last five.
people: With about 23,000 employees, each generates about $508K of revenue, 1.4x the Technology median, and productivity has fallen 3.9% a year.
That works out to $112K of free cash flow per employee.
CEO pay is $6.4M (13x revenue per employee), and compensation governance scores well (1/10, lower is better).
